title: Shepherdsville on Salt River
summary: In 1793 the Kentucky General Assembly established Shepherdsville on Adam Shepherd’s land at the Salt River falls, and it became Bullitt County’s seat.
bodyMarkdown:
Shepherdsville, the seat of Bullitt County, was founded in 1793 on the Salt River near the falls. Its growth was tied to the nearby salt works at Bullitt's Lick, one of Kentucky's earliest industries. Later the railroad, a mineral spa and the interstate each shaped the town.

## Salt country

Native Americans [lived in the area](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shepherdsville,_Kentucky) for at least 15,000 years. European Americans first knew it as Bullitt's Lick, for the salt licks found by the surveyor Thomas Bullitt in 1773. The [Grokipedia article on Shepherdsville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shepherdsville,_Kentucky) says salt making began there in 1777, and the area became home to Kentucky's first commercial salt works, told in [Bullitt's Lick](/stories/bullitts-lick-kentuckys-first-industry/).

Workers boiled brine in large iron kettles, at first 25 kettles of 22 gallons each and later 50. Grokipedia says about 300 gallons of brine made one bushel of salt. Settlement followed, including Brashear's Station, or Salt River Garrison, in 1779, amid ongoing conflict with the Shawnee and other Native nations who opposed settlement.

## Adam Shepherd's town

Adam Shepherd was born in Pennsylvania in 1757 and came to Kentucky around 1781 to survey land for his father, Peter. The town grew around the mill and store Adam built on the Salt River. In 1793, acting on his father's 900-acre Virginia grant, Shepherd set aside 50 acres on the north bank of the river for a town. Grokipedia says the site lay near the falls, Bullitt's Lick and a crossing of the Wilderness Trail.

On December 11, 1793, the Kentucky General Assembly established Shepherdsville and named its first trustees. When Bullitt County was formed in 1796, the town became its seat. Grokipedia gives a population of 96 by 1800. The first post office opened in 1806.

## Spa and railroad

The salt works closed around the 1830s, facing competition from the Kanawha River works in present West Virginia. In 1836 a mineral spa called Paroquet Springs opened, drawing visitors who hoped the water would cure their ailments. The hotel burned in 1879, though the water was bottled and sold until 1915.

In the mid-1850s the [Louisville and Nashville Railroad](/stories/louisville-nashville-railroad-opens-the-interior/) built its main line nearby. Union troops guarded its Salt River bridge during the Civil War. Marie Thompson was lynched near Lebanon Junction in 1904. In December 1917 a two-train collision killed about 50 people, the deadliest train wreck in Kentucky history.

## Kentucky today

For most of the 20th century the town's economy rested on farming and county business. The Kentucky Turnpike, now Interstate 65, brought suburban growth in the 1950s as Louisville workers moved out. Shepherdsville had 14,201 residents in the 2020 census, and in 2024 it began a $40 million plan to remake its downtown, parks and streetscapes. Its salt-making past ties it to [Mann's Lick](/stories/manns-lick-louisvilles-salt-town/) and [Drennon Springs](/stories/drennon-springs-salt-works/).
